prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We show that there is an hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties of sets in a closed symplectic manifold: some sets cannot be displaced by symplectomorphisms from more sets than the others. We also find new examples of rigidity of intersections involving, in particular, specific fibers of moment maps of Hamiltonian torus actions, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds (following the works of P.Albers and P.Biran-O.Cornea), as well as certain, possibly singular, sets defined in terms of Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. In addition, we get some geometric obstructions to semi-simplicity of the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds. The proofs are based on the Floer-theoretical machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states.

outputs.L3:
There is a hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties for subsets of closed symplectic manifolds. In this hierarchy, different sets exhibit different degrees of resistance to displacement by symplectomorphisms. More rigid sets cannot be displaced from a larger class of subsets, while less rigid sets may only be forced to intersect certain special sets. Thus, intersection rigidity provides a way to compare subsets according to how strongly symplectic topology constrains their possible positions under Hamiltonian or symplectic transformations.

A central theme is that some subsets of a symplectic manifold are “more non-displaceable” than others. In particular, a set may be impossible to displace not only from itself, but also from many other subsets. This leads to refined notions of rigidity that go beyond ordinary non-displaceability. Rather than asking only whether a set can be moved off itself, one studies how large the family of sets is from which it cannot be displaced. This perspective reveals a rich structure in the symplectic topology of closed manifolds.

The work produces new examples of such intersection-rigid sets. These include certain fibers of moment maps, which arise naturally in Hamiltonian group actions and integrable systems. It also includes monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, a class of Lagrangians that plays a central role in Floer theory and quantum topology. In addition, the results apply to specific subsets defined by Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. Since functions in such subalgebras pairwise Poisson commute, they determine integrable-type structures, and their fibers can display strong intersection rigidity.

Another important outcome is the identification of geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of quantum homology in symplectic manifolds. Quantum homology is an algebraic invariant encoding both classical topology and counts of pseudo-holomorphic curves. Its semi-simplicity has significant consequences in symplectic topology, particularly in the construction of quasi-states and quasi-morphisms. The results show that the existence or behavior of certain rigid subsets can obstruct this algebraic property, thereby linking geometric intersection phenomena with the algebraic structure of quantum homology.

The proofs rely on Floer-theoretical tools, especially the machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states. These quasi-states are functionals on spaces of smooth functions that behave linearly on Poisson-commutative subspaces and satisfy monotonicity-type properties. They are derived from spectral invariants in Hamiltonian Floer theory and provide a powerful method for detecting rigidity. Through partial symplectic quasi-states, one can prove that certain subsets must intersect under symplectic transformations and establish the hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties described above.
outputs.L4:
This text investigates a hierarchy of intersection rigidity phenomena in closed symplectic manifolds. The central theme is the study of subsets that cannot be displaced, or cannot be separated from certain other subsets, by Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms or more general symplectomorphisms. These rigidity properties are organized into a systematic framework, ranging from classical non-displaceability to stronger forms of “heaviness,” “superheaviness,” and related intersection constraints.

A key tool in the analysis is the theory of Floer-theoretical partial symplectic quasi-states and quasi-morphisms. These objects, which arise from spectral invariants in Hamiltonian Floer theory and quantum homology, allow one to extract robust information about the interaction between symplectic dynamics and the topology of subsets of a symplectic manifold. In particular, quasi-states provide a mechanism for detecting sets that must intersect their Hamiltonian images, or that must intersect other rigid sets under all symplectic transformations of a prescribed type.

The text develops a unified approach to several classes of examples. One important source of rigid subsets comes from moment maps and Poisson-commutative families of functions. Fibers of such maps often exhibit strong intersection properties, and the text identifies conditions under which these fibers are heavy or superheavy with respect to suitable Floer-theoretical quasi-states. This yields new examples of symplectically rigid subsets in manifolds equipped with Hamiltonian torus actions or, more generally, integrable systems.

Another major class of examples involves monotone Lagrangian submanifolds. Using Floer homology and its interaction with ambient quantum homology, the text proves that certain monotone Lagrangians cannot be displaced and, in some cases, enjoy stronger rigidity properties. These results extend known non-displaceability theorems and clarify the relationship between Lagrangian Floer-theoretic non-vanishing, idempotents in quantum homology, and the heaviness or superheaviness of the underlying Lagrangian.

The discussion also emphasizes Poisson-commutative constructions. Given a finite-dimensional space of mutually Poisson-commuting functions, one can study the fibers of the corresponding moment-type map. The text shows that, under appropriate hypotheses, at least one fiber must be rigid in a strong sense. This provides a general method for producing new examples of non-displaceable and stably non-displaceable subsets, even in settings where explicit geometric descriptions of the fibers may be difficult.

Beyond producing examples, the text derives structural consequences for the algebraic side of symplectic topology. In particular, it shows that the existence or non-existence of certain rigid subsets imposes restrictions on the semi-simplicity of quantum homology. Since partial symplectic quasi-states and quasi-morphisms are closely tied to idempotents and field factors in quantum homology, geometric displacement phenomena can obstruct the decomposition of quantum homology into semi-simple pieces. Thus, intersection rigidity becomes a tool not only for studying subsets of symplectic manifolds, but also for detecting algebraic features of the quantum product.

Overall, the text presents a Floer-theoretic framework for understanding symplectic rigidity through partial quasi-states, develops new families of rigid examples involving moment map fibers, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, and Poisson-commutative systems, and demonstrates how these geometric phenomena reflect and constrain the algebraic structure of quantum homology.
outputs.L5:
In mathematical physics, the **Lagrangian** and **Hamiltonian** formalisms are two fundamental ways of describing the dynamics of a physical system. The Lagrangian approach begins with a function usually defined as the difference between kinetic and potential energy. From this function, the equations of motion are obtained through the principle of least action, which states that a system follows the path for which the action is stationary.

The **Hamiltonian** formulation offers a different but closely related perspective. Instead of focusing on positions and velocities, it uses positions and momenta as the main variables. The Hamiltonian often represents the total energy of the system and leads to Hamilton’s equations, which are especially important in classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and symplectic geometry.

The name **Albers** is associated with modern mathematical work in areas connected to Hamiltonian dynamics and symplectic topology. Researchers such as Peter Albers have contributed to the study of Hamiltonian systems, variational methods, and related geometric structures. In this context, the interaction between Lagrangian submanifolds and Hamiltonian flows becomes a central theme. A Lagrangian submanifold is a special geometric object inside a symplectic manifold, and Hamiltonian dynamics describes how such objects may move or transform over time.

Together, the concepts of **Hamiltonian**, **Lagrangian**, and the work connected with **Albers** illustrate the deep relationship between physics and geometry. They show how abstract mathematical structures can provide powerful tools for understanding motion, energy, and the evolution of complex systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a symplectic geometry paper about intersection rigidity, moment map fibers, monotone Lagrangians, Poisson-commutative subalgebras, and partial symplectic quasi-states.
counterfactuals.output:
We study intersection rigidity phenomena for fibers of moment maps arising from finite-dimensional Poisson-commutative subalgebras on closed symplectic manifolds. Using partial symplectic quasi-states and the associated quasi-measures, we identify a class of fibers that are nondisplaceable and, in many cases, stably nondisplaceable. Our approach gives a unified criterion detecting rigid fibers in integrable and partially integrable systems, extending known results for toric moment maps and heavy/superheavy subsets.

A central role is played by monotone Lagrangian submanifolds contained in moment map fibers. We prove that, under suitable monotonicity and Floer-theoretic nonvanishing assumptions, such Lagrangians force the ambient fiber to be heavy with respect to an appropriate partial quasi-state. Consequently, the fiber has nontrivial intersection with every Hamiltonian image of any superheavy set, and in particular cannot be displaced by Hamiltonian isotopies. We also establish persistence results under perturbations of the Poisson-commutative subalgebra and describe applications to families of singular fibers.

The results provide new examples of rigid fibers beyond the toric setting and clarify the relationship between symplectic quasi-states, Lagrangian Floer theory, and the geometry of moment maps. In particular, we obtain intersection rigidity statements for monotone Lagrangian tori and related singular Lagrangian skeleta in several natural symplectic manifolds. Our methods suggest a general framework in which partial symplectic quasi-states serve as a bridge between algebraic structures in quantum homology and geometric rigidity of integrable systems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a research article proving a hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties in closed symplectic manifolds using Floer theory.
counterfactuals.output:
The article’s main contribution is to organize several “intersection rigidity” phenomena in closed symplectic manifolds into a genuine hierarchy and to prove the hierarchy using Floer-theoretic methods.

In broad terms, it shows that there are different strengths of symplectic non-displaceability, ranging from ordinary Hamiltonian non-displaceability to much stronger forms detected by Floer/quantum invariants.

Main results include:

1. **A hierarchy of rigidity properties**

   The paper defines or systematizes a sequence of intersection properties for subsets or submanifolds of a closed symplectic manifold, for example properties of the form:

   - a set cannot be displaced from itself by a Hamiltonian isotopy;
   - it must intersect certain Hamiltonian images of other sets;
   - it remains non-displaceable after stabilization or product operations;
   - it is detected by spectral invariants, quasi-states, or idempotents in quantum cohomology;
   - it satisfies a stronger “heavy” or “superheavy”-type condition.

   These properties are shown to satisfy implications such as

   \[
   \text{strong rigidity} \Rightarrow \text{stable rigidity} \Rightarrow \text{Hamiltonian non-displaceability},
   \]

   with intermediate levels distinguished carefully.

2. **Floer-theoretic criteria for rigidity**

   The central technical tool is Floer theory. The article relates intersection properties to algebraic structures such as:

   - Hamiltonian Floer cohomology;
   - quantum cohomology;
   - spectral invariants;
   - pair-of-pants products;
   - idempotents or field factors in quantum cohomology;
   - open–closed or closed–open maps in the Lagrangian setting.

   The upshot is that certain nonzero Floer-theoretic classes force geometric intersection results. In particular, if a subset or Lagrangian carries a nontrivial Floer-theoretic invariant, then Hamiltonian isotopies cannot separate it in the prescribed way.

3. **Implications between known notions**

   The paper clarifies how previously known rigidity notions fit together. For instance, notions analogous to heaviness, superheaviness, stable non-displaceability, and ordinary non-displaceability are placed in a single framework.

   A typical conclusion is that stronger Floer-theoretic conditions imply stronger intersection properties. For example, a “superheavy” object intersects every “heavy” object, while heaviness implies stable non-displaceability and hence ordinary non-displaceability.

4. **Strictness of the hierarchy**

   The hierarchy is not merely formal: the article provides examples showing that the implications are generally strict. That is, there are subsets or Lagrangians that are non-displaceable but fail stronger rigidity properties, and others that satisfy an intermediate property without satisfying the strongest one.

   These examples demonstrate that the different levels of rigidity capture genuinely different symplectic phenomena.

5. **Product and stabilization results**

   The article proves that several rigidity properties behave well under products. For example, if two subsets satisfy suitable Floer-theoretic rigidity conditions in two closed symplectic manifolds, then their product satisfies a corresponding condition in the product manifold.

   Such results are important because stable non-displaceability is often stronger than ordinary non-displaceability and is naturally formulated using products with other symplectic manifolds.

6. **Applications to concrete symplectic manifolds**

   The theory is applied to familiar classes of closed symplectic manifolds, such as monotone symplectic manifolds, toric manifolds, projective spaces, or products of such spaces. In these settings, the relevant quantum cohomology and spectral invariants can often be computed explicitly, yielding concrete examples of rigid subsets or Lagrangians.

7. **Conceptual significance**

   The article shows that intersection rigidity is not a single yes/no property. Instead, closed symplectic manifolds contain a layered structure of rigidity phenomena, with Floer theory providing the algebraic mechanism that detects and separates the different layers.

   In short, the main message is:

   > Floer-theoretic invariants organize symplectic intersection rigidity into a hierarchy, and this hierarchy has both nontrivial implications and genuinely distinct levels.

counterfactuals.output:
We study rigidity phenomena for subsets of symplectic manifolds through the lens of partial symplectic quasi-states. Given a closed symplectic manifold, we investigate criteria ensuring that a subset cannot be displaced from itself, or from another subset, by Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms. Our approach uses the quasi-linearity and vanishing properties of partial symplectic quasi-states, together with their associated notions of heaviness and superheaviness, to derive nondisplaceability results for a broad class of subsets.

In particular, we show that subsets on which a partial symplectic quasi-state attains extremal values exhibit strong symplectic rigidity: superheavy sets are nondisplaceable from all heavy sets, and in particular from themselves. We apply these principles to construct and detect new examples of nondisplaceable sets arising from moment-map fibers, level sets of Poisson-commuting functions, and singular subsets associated with integrable systems. The resulting criteria depend only on function-theoretic data encoded by the quasi-state and therefore provide an effective method for proving nondisplaceability without explicit Floer-theoretic computations.

These results further clarify the relationship between partial symplectic quasi-states, Hamiltonian dynamics, and symplectic rigidity. They demonstrate that quasi-state techniques provide a flexible framework for identifying subsets that remain immovable under symplectomorphisms, contributing to the broader program of understanding rigidity versus flexibility in symplectic topology.
